subject: Fitting an ODE model with stan

messages.author: 5a6813b53f047fd4
messages.subject: Fitting an ODE model with stan
parts:
I've got stan up and running and I love it.

I'm working with an ODE model of cellular metabolism (~10 reactions and ~50 parameters some of which are known pretty accurately some not at all).  I have C code to time integrate the equations for a given set of parameters.  I want to fit a model where the likelihood is normal centered at the ODE solution.

Is there a way to do this using stan's modeling language?  If not, I'd be happy to look into interfacing with the source code, but I'd need some pointers about where to start.  How can I use stan's implementation of hmc?

Thanks!

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Fitting an ODE model with stan
parts:
On Friday, October 26, 2012 10:52:50 AM UTC-4, José Rojas Echenique wrote:
I'm working with an ODE model of cellular metabolism (~10 reactions and ~50 parameters some of which are known pretty accurately some not at all).  I have C code to time integrate the equations for a given set of parameters.  I want to fit a model where the likelihood is normal centered at the ODE solution.

I am guessing this would be difficult. One of the things that makes Stan's implementation of HMC great is that it uses auto-differentiation to calculate the gradient of the log posterior with respect to the parameters. However, if your problem requires sending the parameters to an external subroutine, then somehow you have got to slip the derivatives back into the right places when the baton is passed back to Stan.

In general, you might have a model something like this

data {
  ...
}
parameters {
  ...
}
transformed parameters {
  real mu[K];
  mu <- SomeFunctionOfParameters();
}
model {
  // optional priors
  outcome ~ normal(mu,sigma);
}

The above works fine in Stan iff SomeFunctionOfParameters() is explicit (and utilizes functions that are available in Stan). We have talked about adding support for solving for the root of an arbitrary implicit function and teaching Stan implicit differentiation, but there isn't a firm plan on that yet.

There was someone else who was interested in ODEs and Stan. Bob would remember the name. If you really, really wanted to implement the infrastructure to make it work in Stan, it would probably be good to coordinate efforts because it would be a big undertaking.

Ben

parts:
This would likely have to be implemented directly in C++
(http://mc-stan.org/cpp-quickstart.html) as a new model by coding up
the gradients explicitly (derivatives with respect to the parameters
would just give new ODEs on which you should be able to use the same
integrator). This way Stan can proceed with HMC without dealing with
the autodiff problems.

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Fitting an ODE model with stan
parts: On Mon, Oct 29, 2012 at 2:46 PM, Matt Hoffman <mdho...@cs.princeton.edu> wrote:

An alternative might be to build a templated implementation of the ODE
solver in c++ that replaces every instance of the typename double with
a template parameter T. Then Stan could do autodiff on the solver.
(That's right, isn't it?)

Yeah, that's right although the gradients may not be great depending on the solver.  Simple solvers (like Euler integration) could be done directly in the Stan modelling language without too much trouble and would work just fine.  More complex ones (like adaptive stepsize methods, implicit integrators, etc) would have some discontinuities which could hurt.  That said, I'd expect them to work OK.

However, the cost in both time and memory could well be prohibitive.
Implementing the derivatives by hand would certainly be much faster,
if it's feasible.

The cost, particularly for implicit methods, would be quite expensive and could be avoided with clever hand-calculated derivatives.

All of this said, ODE fitting can often be reformulated in terms of fitting temporal derivatives of your data in which case you're not at all required to differentiate through the ODE solver.  E.G., if you have dy = f(y,theta) and you want to fit theta given some ys then you can compute the dy's given the ys using finite differences (or, if you want to get fancy, represent them as latent variables...)  and you no longer need to do the forward simulation.

Cheers,
Marcus

Matt

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Fitting an ODE model with stan
parts:
On Tue, Oct 30, 2012 at 4:59 PM, José Rojas Echenique
<jose.i...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> All of this said, ODE fitting can often be reformulated in terms of fitting
>> temporal derivatives of your data in which case you're not at all required
>> to differentiate through the ODE solver.
>
>> E.G., if you have dy = f(y,theta)
>> and you want to fit theta given some ys then you can compute the dy's given
>> the ys using finite differences (or, if you want to get fancy, represent
>> them as latent variables...) and you no longer need to do the forward
>> simulation.
>
> I'm not sure I understand what you mean here. Finite differences?
> Using rates of change of the data as the dy's?

If you have a time series y_0, ..., y_T that you want to fit an ODE dy
= f(y,theta) then one thing you can do is write (using a backwards
difference):

dy_i = (y_{i} - y_{i-1}) / dt

and try to fit the model

dy_i ~ normal(f(y,theta),sigma)

This has a number of drawbacks but avoids many of the issues of
fitting ODEs. If your time step (dt) is sufficiently small for the
phenomena you want to model, then this will tend to work ok.
(Alternatively, if your dt is large and your ODE solver requires many
small steps or high order methods to advance dt, then it's not likely
to work as well.)

Cheers,
Marcus

Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> writes:

> One of our planned research projects is to work with Frederic Bois
> (the toxicologist who developed mcsim) to do diffeq models in Stan. A

Andrew,

One of the neat features Frédéric added to MCSim was the ability to
inline C code. That let me use GSL's various interpolation routines to
create nonlinear functions, which enabled me to do system dynamics (SD)
simulations (/Business Dynamics/, John Sterman, for example) in MCSim.
There's a quick reference card on MCSim and SD on the MCSim Web site at
http://www.gnu.org/software/mcsim/. While there are commercial SD
simulators (and I do like them), MCSim's approach made a real
contribution in modeling and analysis and was the subject of at least
one conference talk I gave.

If that feature could be included when Frédéric works with you to do
diffeq models in Stan, that would be really great. Or perhaps Stan can
already inline GSL calls and other C code, but I haven't seen (or
needed) it yet. The quick reference card shows how one might use that
in creating a model.

Bill
--

Facilitated Systems

I forgot about that problem.

SD relies heavily on tabular descriptions of nonlinear functions; usually with uneven spacing of the argument.  I have tended to use the akima interpolation routine, but sometimes a linear or step interpolation is handy to match the results from some commercial software.  

If odestan (!?) had those three routines in a suitably-licensed implementation, I'd be happy.  If it also had Stineman interpolation, I wouldn't argue. :-)

Bill
